messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Helena Weiss is a 78-year-old public defender who came to treatment months after being assaulted on her way back to her car after court. She had stayed late preparing for the next morning’s hearing, carrying a stack of files through the concrete parking structure she had used for years without much thought. She remembers the echo of footsteps behind her before she could place where they were coming from, and then the shock of a man coming up close enough that she felt trapped before she fully understood what was happening. What has stayed with her most vividly is not a complete story she tells from beginning to end, but the bodily certainty she had in that moment that someone behind her could become dangerous without warning.

Since then, Helena moves through the world as if that danger could reappear at any time. In the courthouse corridors, where clients, deputies, and families pass in tight streams, she finds herself turning her head to check behind her again and again, especially when she hears steps matching her own. She does the same in the parking garage after work and even in grocery store aisles if a cart seems to trail her for too long. She knows other people may not notice, but she is constantly scanning the space behind her, unwilling to trust that if someone meant to approach her she would otherwise have enough warning.

She also watches other people closely for signs that they might harm her. In the courtroom holding area, she studies faces, hands, posture, and movement with unusual intensity, trying to decide who seems agitated, who is lingering too long, who might suddenly come too near. Because she works as a public defender, much of her day unfolds in settings filled with strangers under stress, and she has begun to feel that she must read every shift in expression to stay safe. If a man raises his voice in the hallway or steps into her path too abruptly, her attention narrows to him immediately. She does not describe this as irrational. From her point of view, this is simply what a person should do after learning how quickly ordinary surroundings can turn dangerous.

Helena is also markedly jumpy. A closing door in chambers, a clerk appearing beside her desk before she has heard them approach, or her husband coming up behind her in the kitchen can make her flinch hard enough to embarrass her. She feels a rapid jolt through her chest and shoulders before she can remind herself where she is. She has begun apologizing reflexively at work when this happens, smoothing it over with humor, though privately she feels unsettled by how little control she has over it. The startle itself frightens her almost as much as the noise or movement that sets it off; it makes her feel exposed, as if her body is still braced for something terrible to happen.

At home, her husband has noticed that she prefers to sit where she can see entrances and dislikes having anyone walk behind her unexpectedly. In meetings at the office, she chooses the chair with the clearest line of sight to the door and to the people around her. These habits are now woven into the fabric of her days. They are not dramatic, but they consume attention, and by the end of the workday she often feels worn down from the effort of staying alert. Even so, she is reluctant to let that vigilance go. She has come to believe that relaxing, even briefly, would be the same mistake as before.

What finally brought Helena in was not a single worsening symptom so much as the realization that her world had become organized around anticipation of threat. After nearly six decades in the law, she takes pride in being composed, formidable, and useful to other people in crisis. Lately, though, she has found herself entering her own workplace with the same bodily readiness she once reserved for genuinely dangerous moments. She is seeking help because she does not want the rest of her life narrowed by this constant watchfulness. What frightens her most is the thought that she may never again feel fully safe with her back turned, even in ordinary places, and what she hopes for is not to forget what happened but to stop living as if it is always about to happen again.
